title: Route 66: The 100-Year-Old Road That Still Makes People Sing
summary:
Imagine a road so famous that people sing songs about it. That's Route 66! This year, America's most legendary highway turns 100 years old.

Route 66 was officially born on November 11, 1926. It stretched about 2,400 miles — from Chicago, Illinois, all the way to Los Angeles, California. People nicknamed it the "Mother Road." It connected eight states: Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California.

Back then, many of those roads were bumpy and broken. Workers slowly fixed them up. By 1938, the whole route was paved smooth.

Route 66 became a lifeline during the Great Depression, a time when millions of Americans lost their jobs. Terrible dust storms ruined farms in the middle of the country. Thousands of families packed their cars and drove west on Route 66, hoping for a better life in California.

After World War II, road trips became super popular. Diners, motels, gas stations, and weird roadside attractions popped up everywhere. The highway meant freedom and adventure.

But in 1956, the government started building bigger, faster interstate highways. They bypassed old Route 66. In 1985, it was officially removed from the U.S. Highway System.

Guess what? The road didn't disappear. Communities worked to save it. Now, all eight states are throwing festivals, car shows, and concerts. A documentary tour started September 3 and ends in Los Angeles on November 7, 2026. Happy 100th birthday, Mother Road!
why_it_matters: Route 66 shows how a road can tie families and small towns together, just like the highways, buses, or train lines that connect your own town to places far away.

questions.question: What nickname did people give Route 66?
Why did thousands of families drive west on Route 66 during the Great Depression?
options: They were going on holiday to Chicago
They hoped for a better life in California
They were building new interstate highways
They wanted to see the new diners and motels
questions.correct_answer: They hoped for a better life in California

questions.question: What happened to Route 66 in 1985?
options: The whole route was finally paved smooth
The first interstate highways were built on it
It was officially removed from the U.S. Highway System
questions.correct_answer: It was officially removed from the U.S. Highway System

questions.question: What are the eight states doing for the road's 100th birthday?
options: Building a new interstate beside it
Holding festivals, car shows, and concerts
questions.correct_answer: Holding festivals, car shows, and concerts

background_read: Route 66 was so famous that a songwriter named Bobby Troup wrote a hit song about it in 1946 called '(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66,' and a TV show with the same name was on American television in the 1960s.
The Great Depression (a time in the 1930s when banks closed and millions of people had no work) hit the middle of the United States especially hard, which is why so many families headed west.
Chicago is a big city in Illinois on the shore of Lake Michigan, and Los Angeles is a huge city in southern California — Route 66 linked these two very different parts of the country.
Article_Structure: WHO: Route 66 — nicknamed the 'Mother Road' — along with the travellers who used it and the communities in the eight states it crossed
WHAT: America's most legendary highway turns 100 years old, and all eight states are celebrating with festivals, car shows, and concerts
WHERE: From Chicago, Illinois, to Los Angeles, California, passing through Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California
WHY: Route 66 was a lifeline of hope during the Great Depression and after World War II it stood for freedom and adventure — so people fought to save it

perspectives.description: The road tells the story of America — the hard years of the Great Depression, the fun road trips after World War II, and the arrival of fast interstate highways.
Birthday festivals and car shows bring visitors who buy food and stay in motels, which helps diners and shops along the old route stay open.
Interstate highways are faster and get people where they need to go quickly, so most drivers today would not want to take the slow, winding old road every day.
